🛠️ Understanding Your Node.js Environment: What That Long Path Actually Means

Ever run `which node` and see something like `/Users/user/.nvm/versions/node/v22.19.0/bin/node`?

That's not just a random path — it's telling you exactly how your development environment is set up.

Let me break it down:

📍 `/Users/user/.nvm/` — You're using NVM (Node Version Manager)
📍 `versions/node/v22.19.0/` — Currently running Node.js version 22.19.0
📍 `bin/node` — The actual executable file

⸻

Why this matters for developers:

✅ **Version Management**: NVM lets you switch between Node versions instantly
✅ **Project Isolation**: Different projects can use different Node versions
✅ **No Permission Issues**: Installed in user space, not system-wide

Compare this to a system-wide installation:
`/usr/local/bin/node` — installed globally, harder to manage versions

⸻

Quick NVM commands I use daily:

• `nvm list` — See all installed versions
• `nvm use 18.17.0` — Switch to specific version
• `nvm install --lts` — Install latest LTS version
• `nvm alias default 22.19.0` — Set default version

⸻

This setup has saved me countless hours when working on projects that require different Node versions.

No more "works on my machine" issues when the team uses different Node versions.

⸻
